## Source Extractor

Research question: "Research state-of-the-art and NOVEL techniques for a FAST BATCHED SQUARE Householder QR factorization on an NVIDIA B200 (sm_100, Blackwell, TF32/tf32x3 tensor cores, CUDA 12.8, Triton 3.6 + Gluon/TLX, PyTorch 2.11), written as CUSTOM kernels (Triton first, CUDA/CuTe DSL for more control — NOT library calls). I have an existing blocked compact-WY implementation at 2388us geomean (rank #5); competitors WITHOUT NVFP4 reach ~1360us (1.3-1.8x faster), so reachable headroom provably exists. I need techniques to BEAT it, and I may need to invent new ones — propose novel combinations, not just a catalog.

EXACT OUTPUT CONTRACT (this is the binding constraint): output must be packed (H, tau) such that a checker computes Q = torch.linalg.householder_product(tril(H,-1), tau), R = triu(H), and requires (in FP64): ||R - Q^T A|| <= 20*n*eps32 * ||A||, ||Q^T Q - I|| <= 100*n*eps32, and tril(Q^T A, -1) ~ 0. So ANY valid FLAT global Householder representation (H, tau) passes — it need NOT match LAPACK bit-for-bit, but Q must be A's true orthogonal factor and the reflectors must compose as ONE global householder_product sequence (per-panel/per-block reflectors that don't compose globally FAIL). Inputs include ill-conditioned, rank-deficient, near-rank-deficient, clustered-singular-value, near-collinear, banded, and row-scaled matrices, so the method must be numerically robust (naive CholeskyQR that squares the condition number FAILS the ill-conditioned cases).

THE BOTTLENECK: after optimizing the trailing-update GEMMs (already at tensor-core roofline / minimal-MMA round-to-nearest precision), the PANEL FACTORIZATION (the tall-skinny n x IB QR with its SERIAL reflector-by-reflector dependency chain) is now ~45% of runtime and is the critical path. The dominant shapes are batch=640/n=512, batch=60/n=1024 (grid-starved: 60 thread-blocks on 148 SMs leaves most idle during the panel), batch=8/n=2048, batch=2/n=4096.

I need, with code-level specificity and URL citations:
1. HOUSEHOLDER RECONSTRUCTION from communication-avoiding QR: the LAPACK xORHR_COL / xUNHR_COL routine and the Ballard-Demmel-Grigori-Hoemmen-Knight (2014/2015) "Reconstructing Householder vectors from TSQR" method. How to make the reconstruction step CHEAP (it is currently O(batch * n^3) and eats the panel savings) — can the reconstruction itself be tensor-core GEMM-heavy and parallel? Exact recurrences.
2. TSQR / CAQR (communication-avoiding QR): the row-block-tree panel factorization that replaces the serial reflector chain with O(log P) tree-reduction, filling idle SMs at grid-starved batch. How to combine TSQR (which gives R + an implicit Q) with ORHR_COL to emit FLAT geqrf-compatible (H, tau). Per-leaf and merge recurrences; how to map the tree to one-CTA-per-row-block on a GPU without O(n) device-wide barriers.
3. PANEL CRITICAL-PATH SHORTENING that is NOT communication-avoiding: the UT-transform / compact-WY-T-only formulation, recursive/divide-and-conquer panel (geqrt3), look-ahead, and any 2023-2026 GPU technique that shortens the serial Householder dependency chain length (not just GEMM-ifies the trailing apply).
4. BATCHED QR specifically: MAGMA batched geqrf, cuSOLVER batched, and any recent (2023-2026) papers on batched small/medium QR on tensor-core GPUs — what algorithm do they use for the panel, and how do they handle the batch=640/n=512 (GPU-saturating) vs batch=2/n=4096 (GPU-starved) regimes differently?
5. MIXED-PRECISION robust QR: tf32x3/error-corrected-TF32 and 3xTF32 emulation for the panel reflector formation (not just the trailing), and iterative refinement / re-orthogonalization schemes that keep flat-(H,tau) FP32 accuracy on ill-conditioned/rank-deficient inputs.
6. A RANKED list of 3-5 DISTINCT, concrete, buildable approaches (each with the key numerical risk and the cheapest decisive experiment to validate it) to shorten the panel critical path while still emitting exact flat (H, tau) — prioritized for the batch=640/n=512 and batch=60/n=1024 regimes that dominate the geomean. Explicitly include any NOVEL combination you can construct from the above primitives, even if not published."

103	2.1   Nested Blocking
104	A standard QR factorization directly calls the unblocked panel factorization
105	(dgeqr2). For a batch of relatively small matrices, the panel is thin, typically
106	4–8 in most cases. Thin panels lead to rank-k updates (batch GEMM) that are
107	memory-bound. On the other hand, passing relatively wide panels directly to
108	the memory-bound dgeqr2 also hinders the performance. The solution to this
109	tradeoﬀ is to use nested blocking, which is a well-known approach in LAPACK’s
110	blocked algorithms, despite not being used in the standard QR implementation.
111	Figure 2 shows the general idea of nested blocking, where a wide panel is inter-
112	nally split during its factorization. Nested blocking increases the reliance on L3
113	BLAS operations (batch GEMM).

232	5   Panel Optimization
233	We begin by designing a new GPU kernel for the panel factorization. The kernel
234	caches a panel of size m × nb in the register ﬁle of the GPU and implements the
235	unblocked factorization (dgeqr2). In a thread block, each thread possesses one
236	row of the panel, so at least m threads are required for each thread block. There
237	are two occasions where we perform a reduction operation across the columns of
238	the panel. The ﬁrst is during the generation of the Householder reﬂector, where
239	the norm of the current column is computed. The second is when applying the
240	reﬂector to the trailing matrix, i.e., A = (I−τ vv T )×A. The product v T A requires
241	a reduction operation across the columns of A. Since these reductions contradict
242	with the thread-per-row assignment, a shared memory workspace is allocated
243	to perform tree reductions. Note that the v T A product involves a multi-column
244	reduction, for which we re-organize the threads into independent groups, and
245	each group collaboratively reduces the assigned column. A key design aspect of
246	this kernel is the use of compile-time constants. For example, the width of the
247	panel nb must be known at compile time in order to avoid register spilling. It
248	also helps the compiler unroll most of the loops inside the kernel. The kernel is
249	instantiated for 1 ≤ nb ≤ nbmax , where nbmax depends on the GPU resources
250	as well as the compute precision.
251	    The performance of this kernel is dependent on the height of the panel, since
252	it requires one thread per row. For example, a panel of size 512 × nb needs 512
253	threads. Assuming that all other resources are not a bottleneck, we can schedule
254	four thread blocks at maximum per SM, due to a hardware limitation. Panels
255	taller than 512 would cause at least 25% drop in the thread occupancy per SM.
256	Depending on the width of the panel, other resources could be underutilized as
257	well. The remedy to such a behavior is to relax the constraint on the number
258	of threads. We propose a second kernel that stores the panel in shared memory
259	instead. This enables us use any number of threads to factorize the panel. The
260	proposed kernel assumes nb ≤#threads≤ m. The tree reductions mentioned
261	above are redesigned to work with any number of threads in that range. To
262	prove our point, Fig. 4 shows the performance of the two kernels for a panel of
263	width 4. For the shared memory kernel, we use 32, 64, and 128 threads. The
264	ﬁgure shows that there is no clear winner, and that two decisions should be
265	made before the panel factorization: (1) which kernel should be used (register
266	vs. shared memory), and (2) if the shared memory kernel is used, how many
267	threads should be used? All performance graphs in this ﬁgure have a staircase-
268	like behavior. As the panel becomes taller, more resources are required, leading
269	to drops in occupancy. In order to select the best performing kernel, we collect
270	oﬄine tuning data based on panel width, precision, and GPU architecture. These
271	data are used to select such a kernel at run time.

322	6   Optimizing the Trailing Matrix Update
323	We acknowledge that we cannot use the batch dgemm kernel to compute the T
324	factor for relatively thin matrices. At the same time, using the memory bound
325	dgemv and dtrmv kernels is not expected to be a faster solution. Since this
326	improvement is critical mostly for tall-skinny sizes, a candidate solution is to
327	merge the dlarft and the dlarfb operations into one GPU kernel. However,
328	since the fused kernels operate on the fastest memory levels of the GPU, the
329	implementation can be simpliﬁed into applying the elementary reﬂectors directly
330	to the trailing matrix (without forming the T factor). This strategy is partially
331	similar to cuBLAS and KBLAS in the sense that they don’t use the batch GEMM
332	for the trailing matrix update. However, we limit its use for a certain width, as
333	we discuss later in the paper. Algorithm 3 shows a pseudo code of the proposed
334	kernel. It reads the output of dgeqr2 into shared memory, setting its upper
335	triangular part to zeros, and its diagonal to ones. The factorized panel remains
336	cached for the lifetime of the kernel. Assuming that the trailing matrix has a
337	width n̄, we loop over this width in a small step ib, so that the sub-trailing
338	panel (tA[]) is cacheable in either the shared memory or the register ﬁle. We
339	use a device routine implementation of the dlarf routine to apply each reﬂector

346	memory only, and has a tunable number of threads.
